title: Seasonal Depression (SAD): More Than Just Winter Blues
description: Seasonal Affective Disorder is real depression tied to seasons. Causes, light therapy, medication, and other evidence-based treatments.

content.text: Every winter, it hits. The energy drains, the mood drops, the cravings for carbs kick in. If this happens predictably, you may have Seasonal Affective Disorder—and there are effective treatments.
SAD is a subtype of major depression that follows a seasonal pattern:

items: Symptoms begin and end at predictable times each year
Must occur at least 2 consecutive years to diagnose

content.text: About 5% of US adults have SAD. Another 10-20% have milder 'winter blues.'

items: Depressed mood most of the day
Vitamin D (lower levels with less sun exposure)

content.text: Light therapy is as effective as antidepressants for SAD, with faster onset. Best results with 10,000 lux light box for 20-30 minutes each morning.
content.citation: Golden et al., American Journal of Psychiatry, 2005

items: Use within first hour of waking
Don't look directly at light, but keep eyes open
SSRIs work well (often started prophylactically before winter)
Bupropion (Wellbutrin) is FDA-approved for SAD prevention
Can be combined with light therapy
Dawn simulators (alarm clocks that mimic sunrise)
Vitamin D supplementation (evidence mixed but low risk)
Maintain social activities despite urges to isolate

content.text: If you know SAD hits you every year, start light therapy and/or medication in early fall before symptoms begin. Prevention is easier than treatment.

SAD is predictable, which means it's preventable. Light therapy is effective, accessible, and has few side effects. If you dread winter every year, you don't have to white-knuckle through it—treatment works.
